explanations.explanation: It appears that the feature is detecting when a period belongs to a token‐sequence that is an abbreviation or otherwise signals a special “entity boundary” (for example, in “U.S.”, “St. Louis”, or “Oct.”). In these cases the period isn’t acting as a sentence‐end but as part of a formatted or proper name token, so the model’s predictions shift from a more generic continuation (like “vet”) to one that fits a proper noun or numeric entity (such as “S”, “Louis”, “13”, etc.).

explanations.explanation: This feature appears to be detecting a specific subword or morpheme‐segment—often the latter half of a compound or morphologically complex word—that cues the model to complete a proper, context–appropriate word rather than defaulting to a generic continuation.

It appears to be a subword “morpheme‐boundary” detector—one that flags the point in a word where a common inflectional or compound suffix (–es, –ed, –ing, –ies, etc.) begins, helping the model correctly complete word forms in names, technical terms, and other compound words.

explanations.explanation: It detects where a sentence or clause is being neatly “closed” by a period—especially in news‐ or announcement–style language (e.g. after abbreviations like “Jan.” or “St.”). In other words, it signals proper punctuation boundaries that guide the model to continue with linguistically appropriate text.

This feature appears to detect the presence of anomalous or placeholder characters—the Unicode replacement character (�) or its clusters—that are inserted when text contains mis‐encoded or nonstandard symbols. In effect, it flags these “missing” or “corrupted” tokens, which then influence next-token predictions by acting as markers for shifts in content or formatting.
It’s a self‐referential feature—it lights up on first‐person (“I”) expressions that signal the speaker’s personal agency or subjective viewpoint.

It appears that this feature detects when a token is the start of a headline‐ or title–like snippet (such as a product name, ad headline, or listing entry) and, by doing so, shifts the model’s next-token distribution to produce contextually appropriate completions instead of a generic continuation.

It appears this feature encodes a “news‐reporting” or formal journalistic style signal—activated when the context sets up a fact‐based, official, or headline-like statement (often preceding proper names or titles). In its presence the model leans toward a structured, information‐dense continuation (e.g. naming an official or event), whereas without it the fallback is a generic punctuation (a dash).

It appears this feature “lights up” on numeric expressions and their adjoining units or symbols – that is, when the text contains statistics, percentages, durations, or other measurement/quantity formulations. In context, the activated tokens (like “5”, “%”, “last”, “years”, “million”, etc.) signal that the model is in a quantitative mode, which then guides more appropriate next‐token predictions in these measurement or numerical contexts.
